<meta>continues from previous page: as</meta> are usually proposed <margin>Soto, Book IV, question 7, article 2. Covarruvias on the chapter "Sin."</margin> by Soto and by theologians who establish an internal tribunal of the soul <note>original: "internum animi tribunal"</note>. <margin>Part II, section I. Silvestri on the word "Restitution," number 3, question 6.</margin>

III. First, it is evident that a possessor in good faith <term>bonæ fidei poffefforem</term> <gloss>one who believes they are the lawful owner</gloss> (for a possessor in bad faith is liable for his actions beyond the value of the thing itself) is not bound to any restitution if the thing has perished: because the thing itself is not with him, nor has he profited from it.

IV. Second, that a possessor in good faith is bound to restore <margin>Medina on contracts, question 10.</margin> even the existing fruits of the thing: I say fruits of the thing; for fruits of industry <margin>Zeffirini, Book II, chapter 14. Navarro, chapter 17, number 7.</margin>, even if they would not have arisen without the thing, are not owed to the thing. The cause of this obligation is from ownership <term>dominio</term> <gloss>legal title or mastery</gloss>. For he who is the owner of a thing is also naturally the owner of the fruits of that thing.

V. Third, that a possessor in good faith is bound to the restitution of both the thing and the fruits consumed, if he would otherwise have consumed just as much: for in this case, he is considered to have become wealthier. Thus Gaius Caesar Caligula is praised <margin>Suetonius, chapter 16.</margin> regarding the beginnings of his reign, because to those to whom he restored kingdoms, he also added the fruits of the intervening time.

VI. Fourth, that he is not bound for the fruits he neglected to collect: because he neither has the thing, nor anything that takes the place of the thing.

VII. Fifth, if such a possessor has given a thing gifted to him to someone else, he is not bound unless he would have given just as much even without this thing: for then it will be a profit to have spared his own property. <margin>Law "Qui vas," final paragraph, Digest on theft.</margin>

VIII. Sixth, if he has sold a thing he bought, he is not bound, except perhaps to the extent that he sold it for more: but if he sold a gifted thing, he is bound to restore the price, unless perhaps he squandered the price, which he would not have otherwise squandered. <margin>Law "Si et rem," Digest on the petition of inheritance.</margin>

IX. Seventh, that another's property bought in good faith must be restored, and the price paid cannot be recovered <margin>Law "Sed et si lege," Digest, same title.</margin>. To this rule, this exception seems to me to be added: unless the owner probably could not have regained possession of his thing without some expense, for instance, if the thing was among pirates <margin>Law "Si eum servum," Digest on things credited.</margin>. For then, as much as the owner would have been willing to spend can be deducted. For the possession of the fact itself, especially when difficult to recover, is something valuable <margin>Law "Mater tua." Law "Si mancipia." Digest on the recovery of property.</margin>; and in this, the owner is considered to have become wealthier after the thing was lost. And therefore, although the purchase of one's own property is not valid by ordinary law, the Jurist Paulus says that it is valid if it was agreed from the start that the possession, which is with another, should be bought <margin>Law "Sacra," Digest on the contract of sale. Law 1, Digest on evictions.</margin>. Nor do I here require that the thing be bought with the intention that it be restored to the owner—in which case some say an action for business transacted <term>negotiorum actionem</term> <gloss>a claim for expenses incurred on another's behalf without a mandate</gloss> arises <margin>Law "Si laborav," paragraph "Si navis," Digest on the Rhodian Law.</margin>. <margin>Egidio Regio, dispute 35, doubt 7, number 126. Hostiensis, title on penance, on the word: "what concerning those buying booty."</margin>

<note>Note a: Law "Si in emptione," paragraph "rei," Digest on the contract of sale.</note>

<summary>This page outlines the legal and moral obligations of a possessor in good faith regarding the restoration of property and its profits. Grotius defines seven rules for when restitution is required, emphasizing the principle that no one should be unjustly enriched at another's expense.</summary>
<keywords>good faith possession, restitution, fruits of property, ownership, unjust enrichment, maritime law, Caligula, Paulus the Jurist, Roman law</keywords>
